q: You are following the flotilla lead boat across to Kalamos. Your crew say, "Just follow them — they keep watch." What does Rule 5 require?
a: You keep your own lookout at all times
o: The lead boat keeps lookout for all
A lookout only in poor visibility
The AIS alarm counts as a lookout
why: Rule 5: every vessel keeps a proper lookout by sight and hearing at all times.

q: Motoring across the Saronic Gulf, you take a compass bearing of a ferry: 040°, and again 040° five minutes later, and she is closer. What does it mean?
a: Risk of collision exists
o: She will pass safely ahead
She will pass safely astern
She is stopped in the water
why: Rule 7: a steady compass bearing with the range closing means risk of collision.

q: You are the give-way boat in a crossing with a motor yacht a mile off. How do you alter course?
a: Early and boldly, so she clearly sees it
o: A few degrees at a time, gradually
At the last moment, to keep options open
A little, then speed up to cross ahead
why: Rule 8: action is early, large enough to be obvious, and leaves a safe distance.

q: You are motoring through the narrow Lefkas canal and a tripper boat is coming the other way. Where do you keep?
a: To the starboard side of the channel
o: In the middle, where it is deepest
To the port side, facing the traffic
Either side, as long as you go slowly
why: Rule 9: keep as near the starboard edge of a narrow channel as is safe.

q: Sailing through the narrow strait at Poros, you meet this ferry. Who keeps clear?
a: You — do not impede her in the channel
o: She does — power gives way to sail
She does — she can stop more easily
Neither — both hold course and speed
why: Rule 9(b): a sailing vessel must not impede a vessel that can only navigate in the channel.

fig.note: Narrow channel · she can only use the channel

q: Both yachts are under sail and converging. Who keeps clear?
a: You — you are on port tack
o: She does — she is on port tack
Neither — both alter to starboard
Whichever boat is to windward
why: Rule 12(a)(i): on different tacks, the port-tack boat keeps clear.

q: Under sail, you are converging with this yacht. Who keeps clear?
a: She does — she is to windward
o: You do — you are to leeward
You do — she is on your starboard side
Neither — same tack, both hold on
why: Rule 12(a)(ii): on the same tack, the windward boat keeps clear of the leeward one.

q: You are motoring at night and see these lights. What do you do?
a: Alter to starboard — she is head-on
o: Alter to port, passing starboard to starboard
Hold course — she must keep clear of you
Stop and wait for her to go past
why: Rule 14: a masthead light and both sidelights dead ahead mean head-on; both turn to starboard.

q: You are motoring. What do you do?
a: Hold your course and speed
o: Alter to port and pass ahead of her
Slow right down and let her pass ahead
Alter to starboard and pass astern
why: Rule 15: she has you on her starboard side, so she gives way; you stand on (Rule 17).

q: You are motoring and should stand on, but this yacht is not giving way. What do you do?
a: Sound five short blasts and be ready to act
o: Hold on regardless — the rules protect you
Turn hard to port across her bow
Speed up to get across ahead of her
why: Rules 17 and 34(d): signal doubt, then act yourself — but not by turning to port for her.

fig.note: She has not altered · now close

q: Sailing off Preveza, you are converging with a boat showing this shape. Who keeps clear?
a: You — she is engaged in fishing
o: She does — power gives way to sail
She does — she is on your starboard side
Neither — she is at anchor
why: Rule 18: a sailing vessel keeps clear of a vessel engaged in fishing.

q: You see this yacht with her sails up and this shape hoisted forward. What does it tell you?
a: She is motoring as well as sailing
o: She is at anchor
She is fishing with nets
She cannot manoeuvre easily
why: Rule 25(e): a cone point down shows a yacht under sail and power — treat her as power.

q: This yacht is under sail only. Who keeps clear?
a: You — motor-sailing, you count as power
o: She does — she is on port tack
She does — she is on your port side
Neither — both of you have sails up
why: Rule 3: with the engine in gear you are power-driven, so you keep clear of sail (Rule 18).

fig.note: Your engine is running, in gear

q: Under sail alone, a motor yacht crosses from your starboard side on a steady bearing. Your crew say she has right of way because she is on your starboard side. Who keeps clear?
a: She does — power gives way to sail
o: You do — she is on your starboard side
You do — she is bigger and faster
Both alter course to starboard
why: Rule 18: power keeps clear of sail; the starboard-side rule is for two power vessels.

q: You are motoring at night with the sails stowed. Your yacht has a masthead tricolour, a steaming light on the mast and navigation lights at bow and stern. What do you switch on?
a: Steaming light, sidelights and sternlight
o: The masthead tricolour only
The tricolour and the steaming light
Sidelights and sternlight only
why: Rule 23: under power you show a masthead (steaming) light, sidelights and a sternlight.

q: You are motoring at night and see this single light high up. What is it, and what do you do?
a: A yacht under sail — you keep clear
o: A power boat — you stand on
A starboard-hand buoy — leave it to starboard
A yacht at anchor — pass either side
why: A lone light high on a mast is a tricolour: a yacht under sail, so you, under power, keep clear.

q: In Poros harbour, a ferry near the quay sounds three short blasts. What does she mean?
a: I am operating astern propulsion
o: I am altering my course to starboard
I am altering my course to port
I doubt that you are keeping clear
why: Rule 34(a): one short = to starboard, two = to port, three = astern propulsion.

q: In fog off the Croatian coast you hear one prolonged blast about every two minutes, getting closer. What is it?
a: A power-driven vessel making way
o: A sailing vessel under way
A vessel at anchor
A vessel aground
why: Rule 35(a): a power vessel making way sounds one prolonged blast at least every 2 minutes.

q: You are catching up this yacht from astern. Who keeps clear?
a: You — you are overtaking her
o: She does — she is on port tack
Neither — both hold course and speed
Whichever of you is the larger
why: Rule 13 overrides Rule 12: an overtaking vessel keeps clear, whatever the tacks.

fig.note: You are faster, closing from astern

q: Crossing to Paxos at night under engine, you watch these lights for five minutes. What do you do?
a: Give way — turn to starboard, pass astern
o: Stand on — she must turn to starboard
Turn to port and pass ahead of her
Speed up and cross ahead of her
why: Her red sidelight shows her port side: she is crossing from your starboard, so you give way.

fig.note: Night · on your starboard bow, bearing steady
